items.title: 61521_David Albert Francis oral history interview
items.q: Cab Calloway, I will always feel obligated, in a way, to him, because when I joined his band, I had just left Lucky's band

ctx.x: You came into quite an organized band, of guys who had been traveling for a long time.

The greatest education -- I must admit that. Cab Calloway, I will always feel obligated, in a way, to him, because when I joined his band, I had just left Lucky's band which was a wild band, I mean, when I say, 'wild', guys were not oriented as far as being family men, and a lot of them in the band were married, but they were just like they were single.

But when I joined Cab, I watched the other guys in the band, and I watched the way they used to send money home, because I used to forget to send money home some weeks, because I used to love to gamble, which I didn't know how to gamble, but I still loved to gamble, and I used to lose my money a lot of times, but I noticed guys like Jonah Jones and Milt Henton and Keg Johnson and Hilton Jefferson, these guys, how they would run to the Western Union and send that money home first, and then they would gamble the…

items.title: Panama Francis interviewed by Michael Woods, Los Angeles, California, September 1, 1995
items.q: Later gigs with Billy Hicks, Roy Eldridge, Lucky Millinder and Cab Calloway made him a familiar and sought-after drummer

ctx.x: Drummer David “Panama” Francis has been performing professionally since the 1930’s. A native of Miami, David played his first engagements with the Florida Collegians and in New York with Tab Smith. Later gigs with Billy Hicks, Roy Eldridge, Lucky Millinder and Cab Calloway made him a familiar and sought-after drummer for both recordings and live shows.
